subject: Host-path evaluation: VPC peering vs PrivateLink vs S2S VPN for Private Deploy
messages:
From: Sierra Rogers <sierra.rogers@nexam ed.com>
To: Grace O'Connor <grace.oconnor@redwood.ai>
Cc: netops@nexam ed.com, Tom Hanley <th@edgeconsulting.io>
Date: Thu, 25 Mar 2027 09:12:00 -0700
Subject: Help deciding connectivity path for Redwood Private deployment

Hi Grace —

Thanks again for the intro. We're in the middle of an internal evaluation for hosting Redwood's private deployment in our GCP account. High-level requirements: low-latency API calls from our app (multi-AZ), minimal egress exposure, maintainable audit logging (S3/Cloud Logging), and the ability for our on-prem analytics cluster to pull model logs/metrics at night.

Attached is our current projected VPC layout (nexamed_vpc_diagram_v1.pdf) and a short checklist of compliance needs.

We have three patterns on the table: VPC peering, Private Service Connect / PrivateLink style endpoints, or a site-to-site VPN between our datacenter and the VPC. Can you help highlight tradeoffs and a recommended approach? We're sensitive to both security posture and operational complexity.

Thanks,
Sierra Rogers
Head of Infrastructure | NexaMed

Attachments: nexamed_vpc_diagram_v1.pdf (PDF), connectivity_requirements_checklist.xlsx (XLSX)

From: Rishi Malhotra <rishi.malhotra@redwood.ai>
To: Sierra Rogers <sierra.rogers@nexam ed.com>, Grace O'Connor <grace.oconnor@redwood.ai>
Cc: Karthik Iyer <karthik.iyer@redwood.ai>
Date: Thu, 25 Mar 2027 11:01:00 -0700
Subject: Re: Help deciding connectivity path for Redwood Private deployment

Hi Sierra — thanks for the materials, looks comprehensive. Quick summary from our side: all three options are viable, but they differ on control, telemetry, and failure modes. Below are concise notes so we can align on constraints before Karthik and I sketch config snippets.

- VPC peering:
  * Pros: simple L3 routing, low latency, native GCP peering performance.
  * Cons: no cross-project service-level access controls; transitive routing limitations; requires route exchanges and careful CIDR planning.

- PrivateLink / Private Service Connect:
  * Pros: preserves service-level boundaries, supports per-endpoint IAM/ACLs, hides service behind an endpoint — decouples network from app routing.
  * Cons: slightly higher per-connection cost; can be more operational overhead initially (endpoint lifecycle).

- Site-to-site VPN:
  * Pros: works with on-prem without cloud-native adjustments, good for administrative/analytics access, easy to hand to network team.
  * Cons: variable latency, additional hop, and you'd still want a private path for production traffic for predictable SLOs.

Question: do you expect a single account for all production services, or will Redwood endpoints be in a shared services VPC? That affects our recommendation (peering is okay if you control both sides).

If you're free Friday we can run a short call and Karthik can walk through the tradeoff matrix plus the security/routing snippets.

- Rishi
Principal Solutions Engineer | Redwood Inference

From: Karthik Iyer <karthik.iyer@redwood.ai>
To: Sierra Rogers <sierra.rogers@nexam ed.com>, Rishi Malhotra <rishi.malhotra@redwood.ai>, Grace O'Connor <grace.oconnor@redwood.ai>

Folks — following Rishi's notes, I've sketched a decision rubric and included recommended configuration excerpts. Long-ish but wanted to be explicit.

Decision rubric (weighting for NexaMed): security=40%, latency=30%, ops complexity=20%, cost=10%.

1) Production API calls from web/mobile -> Redwood inference: RECOMMEND PrivateLink (Private Service Connect)
   - Rationale: gives you per-endpoint identity + private IPs inside your VPC; avoids route table complexity. PrivateLink keeps Redwood's compute isolated; you get service-level deny-by-default controls.
   - Implementation notes: create PSC endpoint in your prod VPC, whitelist Redwood endpoint IP ranges, configure endpoint routing to local subnets. Attachments: privatelink-config-snippets.txt (contains a sample IAM binding and route-insertion snippet).

2) Admin plane / analytics / nightly pulls from on-prem: RECOMMEND Site-to-Site VPN + a dedicated VPC peering link for bulk traffic if needed
   - Rationale: use VPN for managed access by your on-prem cluster to pull logs and metrics. If you need predictable throughput for replication jobs, establish a peered VPC between a shared-services VPC and Redwood's service VPC (careful with CIDR overlap). VPN covers cross-domain ops without exposing prod endpoints directly.

3) VPC Peering: USE CASES
   - Good when both VPCs are in your control and you need low-latency natively routed traffic (e.g., internal data plane between services you own). Not ideal when one side (Redwood) requires service encapsulation and per-endpoint controls.

Security and observability notes:
- Mutual TLS for application-level traffic is still recommended even behind PrivateLink.
- VPC flow logs + endpoint logs should be forwarded to your SIEM. We suggest an agent that tags tokens with request IDs so traces join across logs.
- For SOC2: keep a copy of endpoint config, firewall rules, and IAM bindings. We can provide an exportable artifact we use for audits.

Sample snippet (PSC endpoint IAM):
  resources:
    - type: compute.networkEndpointGroup
      name: redwood-psc-neg

Policy fallback plan:
  - If PSC endpoint becomes unavailable, route to a backup endpoint in a second region (multi-region endpoints).

Happy to jump on a call. If you want, we can also run a short lab showing traffic profiles.

—Karthik
Senior Infrastructure Engineer | Redwood Inference

Attachments: privatelink-config-snippets.txt

Thanks Karthik — this is exactly what we needed. A couple follow-ups from security:

1) For PrivateLink endpoints, can you confirm which logs we can ingest into our S3/GCS and whether Redwood retains any request-level logs in your control plane?
2) For the VPN plan, do you recommend dynamic routing (Cloud Router) vs static routes for the initial setup?

We're tentatively leaning to PrivateLink for production API and VPN for on-prem analytics as you suggested. If you can share the SOC2-friendly export and a short runbook for endpoint rotation, we'll prep our security review.

Best,
Sierra

Sierra — good alignment. To answer your security questions:

1) Logs and retention:
   - For PrivateLink traffic, you will receive VPC endpoint flow logs and can configure export to GCS/S3. Redwood also captures anonymized request metadata for billing and performance debugging (request IDs, latency histograms). We do not store customer payloads; payload retention is controllable in the deployment config (default 0 days). We will provide a SOC2 export that includes endpoint ACLs, IAM bindings, and flow-log configuration.

2) VPN routing recommendation:
   - Start with dynamic routing (Cloud Router) if you expect to scale or add on-prem peers. Static routes are fine for a one-off single-site connection but are brittle for failover. Dynamic routing also makes it easier to advertise multiple prefixes (e.g., analytics subnet and management subnet) without manual changes.

Operational next steps (action items):
  - Redwood: produce SOC2 export and endpoint rotation runbook (ETA: 3 business days).
  - NexaMed: confirm whether Redwood will be deployed into a dedicated prod VPC or shared-services VPC (impacts peering/no-peering).
  - Schedule 60-minute lab with Karthik to validate PSC endpoint behavior (let us know times).

I'll attach the export once ready and a short checklist for your security review. Thanks all — sounds like PrivateLink + VPN hybrid is the right path for NexaMed.

Regards,
Grace O'Connor
VP, Solutions | Redwood Inference

Attachments: privatelink-runbook-draft.pdf, SOC2-export-template.json
